bib.title: Efficient Agents: Building Effective Agents While Reducing Cost

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Efficient Agents: Building Effective Agents While Reducing Cost", OPPO AI Agent Team (Ningning Wang, Xavier Hu core; corresponding He Zhu, Wangchunshu Zhou), arXiv 2508.02694v1, preprint, 2025 (arXiv stamp 24 Jul 2025, dated Aug 6 2025). Code: github.com/OPPO-PersonalAI/OAgents.

COVERAGE: 52,942 of 52,942 chars read (all pages, appendices included). References skimmed. The appendix has only the default setup (Table 8) and the memory and Best-of-N judge prompts. The planning prompt it says is in Appendix B is not there. Extraction was clean.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Headline: the tuned "Efficient Agents" config keeps 96.7% of OWL's accuracy at lower cost. The 28.4% is a COST reduction, not a cost-of-pass improvement as the text says.
  number: acc 51.52 vs 53.33; cost $0.285 vs $0.398; cost-of-pass 0.55 vs 0.75.
  setup: GAIA dev set (about 165 tasks by arithmetic), pass@1, GPT-4.1 backbone, config in Table 6. Not call-matched or token-matched: tokens are 127K vs 189K for OWL and 146K for Smolagents. Single run, no variance reported. Per-token prices are May 2025.
  quote: "Efficient Agent (ours) 0.55 0.37 0.54 1.71 51.52 62.26 52.33 26.92 0.285 0.228 0.280 0.461 127K 101K 125K 206K" and "OWL 0.75 0.35 0.80 2.10 53.33 71.70 50.00 26.92 0.398 0.248 0.402 0.566 189K 119K 204K 281K"
  where: Table 7, about char 25,000
- Backbone choice has the largest effect on performance. The most accurate backbone is far from the cheapest per correct answer.
  number: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 61.82% accuracy, cost-of-pass 3.54; GPT-4.1 53.33%, cost-of-pass 0.98; Qwen3-30B-A3B 17.58%, cost-of-pass 0.13.
  setup: same default framework, GAIA dev, six backbones.
  quote: "Claude 3.7 Sonnet achieves the highest accuracy on the GAIA benchmark (61.82% overall) compared to GPT-4.1 (53.33%), but its cost-of-pass is significantly higher (3.54 vs. 0.98)."
  where: Sec 3.1 and Table 1
- Reasoning models get much less efficient on harder tasks.
  number: Claude cost-of-pass L1 1.69 to L3 9.04; o1 1.96 to 12.66.
  setup: GAIA levels 1 to 3, default framework.
  quote: "Claude 3.7 Sonnet's cost-of-pass increases from 1.69 to 9.04 (a 534% surge) and OpenAI o1 from 1.96 to 12.66 (a 646% surge)"
  where: Sec 3.1
- Best-of-N at the step level costs more and gains almost nothing.
  number: N=1 to 4: tokens 243K to 325K, accuracy 53.33 to 53.94, cost-of-pass 0.98 to 1.28.
  setup: N sampled actions per step, scored by a GPT-4o progress reward model. Compared against N=1, so compute is not matched by design. Only N in {1, 2, 4}.
  quote: "accuracy only slightly increasing from 53.33% to 53.94% whenN = 4compared to N = 1. Consequently, this results in a notable decrease in efficiency, with the cost-of-pass rising from 0.98 to 1.28."
  where: Sec 3.2, Table 2
- A cap on ReAct steps helps up to a point. 12 steps is not worth it over 8.
  number: max steps 4/8/12 give cost-of-pass 0.48/0.70/0.98 and accuracy 41.82/52.73/53.33.
  setup: planning interval 1, with a plan generated first and then followed ReAct-style. Interval 1/2/4 at 12 steps gives accuracy 53.33/57.58/53.33, with no clear trend.
  quote: "Beyond a certain threshold, further increasing the maximum steps does not enhance performance but continues to increase costs."
  where: Sec 3.3, Table 3. The text's "58.49% to 69.81%" is the Level 1 column, not overall.
- Simple memory (keep only the observation and action history, no summarisation) is best. LLM-summarised memory costs the most.
  number: simple: accuracy 56.36, cost-of-pass 0.74, 194K tokens. Summarized: 51.52, 1.52, 367K tokens. No-extra baseline: 53.33, 0.98.
  setup: six memory variants, GPT-4.1, GAIA dev. The authors only guess why summarising fails: it "may be due to its inability to accurately summarize past historical trajectories".
  quote: "Simple Memory ... improving from 53.33% (No Extra Memory baseline) to 56.36%, while reducing the cost-of-pass from 0.98 to 0.74."
  where: Sec 3.5, Table 5
- Tool configuration matters for cost. More search sources help on both axes. Static crawling beats page-up/page-down browsing. More query rewrites help.
  number: multi-source vs simple source: cost-of-pass 1.32 to 0.81, accuracy 53.33 to 59.39.
  setup: sources are Google and Wikipedia versus adding Bing, Baidu and DuckDuckGo. Browser variants compared. Query expansion of 3, 5 or 10.
  quote: "the cost-of-pass decreases from 1.32 to 0.81, while accuracy improves from 53.33% to 59.39%."
  where: Sec 3.4, Table 4
- Which components matter, in the authors' words: backbone, max steps and tool use matter most. Best-of-N and memory have negligible effect on accuracy, and redundant versions only add cost.
  quote: "the choice of backbone exerts the most significant impact on the overall system performance."
  where: Sec 3.6
- Metric: cost-of-pass is the cost of one attempt divided by the success rate, with input and output tokens priced separately.
  quote: "It is computed as the ratio of the cost of a single inference attempt, Cm(p), to the success rate,Rm(p)"
  where: Sec 2.2. The extracted formula shows a product; the text says ratio. Table values confirm the ratio: 0.705/0.5333 is about 1.32.
- Selection rule for the final config: "for each component in the agent system, we adopt the configuration with the lowest cost-of-pass among those that do not lead to substantial performance degradation."
  Final config: GPT-4.1, max 8 steps, plan interval 1, multi source, 5 queries, BoN 1, simple memory (Table 6).

LIMITS
- GAIA dev only (about 165 tasks), one run per cell, no confidence intervals. Differences of 1 to 3 points (for example 53.33 vs 53.94) are within noise for n of about 165.
- One component is varied at a time from the default. Interactions are not tested, and the final config is never ablated against the single-change variants.
- Cost-of-pass is estimated from the same accuracy that is being compared. The frameworks are not call-matched. The OWL and Smolagents numbers use each framework's own defaults, and the paper does not say which backbone they used.
- Prices are May 2025. Models and prices have dated since.
- Tool study covers the web browser only. Planning and memory are simple custom designs. The paper itself says the conclusion text has a placeholder ("reducing the operational cost by xx times").
- Authors concede nothing under a limitations heading. The abstract says 'adapts complexity to the task', but the config is fixed, not adaptive.

BUILDS ON: cost-of-pass [20, 27] (Erol et al. is the likely source; check the reference list, I did not confirm the author names); GAIA [19]; OWL [21]; Smolagents [40]; ReAct [37]; Best-of-N [36]; Token-Budget-Aware Reasoning (Han et al. 2024); AgentPrune (Zhang et al. 2024); BudgetMLAgent (Gandhi et al. 2025); overthinking [31]; DistilBERT [15].

CODE: none. The appendix gives prompts only: the memory prompt and the PRM-score and PRM-list judge prompts.

FIGURES: Fig 1 (p.2, component-wise cost-of-pass overview) and Fig 2 (p.4, accuracy vs cost for six backbones). Fig 2 is the better candidate for a note on cost per task. I did not run the captions script; the captions come from the text only.

PROBLEMS
- Internal inconsistencies:
  1. The abstract says cost "from $0.398 to $0.228", but $0.228 is the Level 1 cost; the overall cost is $0.285. The 28.4% matches 0.285/0.398, which is a cost reduction. The cost-of-pass drop is 0.75 to 0.55, which is 26.7%.
  2. GPT-4.1 overall cost is $0.705 in Tables 1, 3 and 4 but $0.521 in Tables 2 and 5, for the same config. Cost-of-pass 0.98 matches $0.521. Table 4's first row has cost-of-pass 1.32 for that same config, which matches $0.705.
  3. o1 shows 69K tokens at $1.908, which looks implausible next to the others.
  4. The text says Efficient Agents "retains 96.7%", but 51.52/53.33 is 96.6%.
  5. Table 4's first row (simple source, crawler, 10 queries) uses the Table 8 default and shows 0.705 and 243K, but its cost-of-pass differs from Table 1.
- No embedded instructions found.
